decisions.text: Agent rulings under his answer, his to undo. (1) 'Every sparking end' is taken literally: any live Terminal end that sparks, also a run the player simply stopped laying, not only a destroyed cell (CordBuilder draws both alike). (2) A floor end's contact is its own cell, 'the sparking end'; the rest of the cord stays harmless. Downed wires keep their present ground contact. (3) Safe = the pawn's construction job (delivering material to or building) targets the conduit blueprint or frame that joins THIS end; a constructor on any other job is shocked, like the re-string case in coverage gap 1. (4) 'Only downed lines' = today's contact set, FlowWorks' collapsed-deck cords included; None = no shock from any wire. (5) The fuel-ignition switch is separate and not widened to floor ends; he spoke of shock only. (6) Shock follows the end's live state at the last 250-tick poll and never the maxSparkingEnds spark budget, which caps only the sparks drawn in view: a live end left out of the spark set still shocks, a dead end never does. Turning the aerial master off must not silence floor ends under All (RebuildContacts returns early on AerialSettings.enabled today).

root_draft.text: Gimme Some Slack hides the tidy conduit and draws in its place what a scavenger base really looks like: too-long extension cords sprawling across the floor in loose loops and coils, piling against walls, plugging into power strips (or connectors, in the other three looks) at every three- or four-way junction, and sagging overhead lines strung between masts. The mess is honest: every cord explains a real power connection, a cut line lies on the ground sparking where it is live and dead where it is not, and nothing is drawn that is not wired. Even a huge base with many wires and connectors shows no problematic delay. Around that look ride a few consequences, all built: a colonist re-strings a cut span, a clamp on a neighbour's line steals their power with a steady goodwill drain if caught, and (built, not yet in his words) a live fallen wire shocks whoever touches it. Judged first: one room of floor cords meeting at a strip, and one cut that leaves a sparking live end and a dead end, with the drawing true to the grid in both.
root_draft.speaker: agent

root.text: Gimme Some Slack hides the tidy conduit and draws in its place what a scavenger base really looks like: too-long extension cords sprawling across the floor in loose loops and coils, piling against walls, plugging into power strips (or connectors, in the other three looks) at every three- or four-way junction, and sagging overhead lines strung between masts. The mess is honest: it faithfully represents connectivity but not the precise conduit path. Every cord explains a real power connection, nothing is drawn that is not wired, and a cut line lies on the ground sparking where it is live and dead where it is not. Even a huge base with many wires and connectors shows no problematic delay. Around that look ride a few consequences, all built: a clamp on a neighbour's line steals their power with a steady goodwill drain if caught; a live fallen wire shocks whoever touches it; and a colonist re-strings a cut span. A pawn who approaches a sparking line intending to fix it is safe; one who incidentally goes over the sparking end on a different job (or anyone else) gets shocked. Judged first: one room of floor cords meeting at a strip, and one cut that leaves a sparking live end and a dead end, with the drawing true to the grid's connectivity in both.
root.speaker: owner
root.quote: Restate Honest: Faithfully represents connectivity but not precise conduit path. For the shock, needs one more line on how a Pawn ever fixes a sparking line: if they approach intending to fix it, they are safe. If they incidentally go over the sparking end with a different job, they (or anyone else) gets shocked.
